procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Magistrate issuing a non-bailable warrant against the appellant, confirmed by the Sessions Court and High Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a criminal revision before the High Court challenging the Magistrate's order. The High Court dismissed the criminal revision.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment of the Patna High Court dismissing his Criminal Revision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the initial refusal by a Magistrate to summon an individual not named in the police charge-sheet amounts to a final discharge, barring subsequent summoning in the same case.

facts: The police investigated a complaint against the appellant and others but accepted the appellant's alibi and did not include him in the charge-sheet.
The Sub-Divisional Magistrate, upon receiving the charge-sheet, noted that the appellant was "discharged."
The case was transferred to another Magistrate who, after hearing testimony from two witnesses that implicated the appellant, issued a warrant to summon him to be tried along with the other accused.
law: A Magistrate takes cognizance of an 'offence', not of the specific 'offenders' named in a police report.
Once a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence, it is their duty to identify all individuals who may be the actual offenders.
The act of summoning an additional accused person is considered a part of the original proceeding that was initiated when the Magistrate first took cognizance of the offence.
application: The Court first determined that the appellant could not have been legally "discharged" because he was never formally an accused person in the first place, as he was not named in the police charge-sheet.
The appellant's argument that the initial refusal to summon him was a final order was rejected on this basis.
The Court reasoned that when the Magistrate took cognizance of the case based on the police report, the entire proceeding related to that offence began.
Therefore, when new evidence (witness testimony) emerged implicating the appellant, the Magistrate had the authority and duty to summon him as part of that same ongoing proceeding.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the initial refusal by a Magistrate to summon an individual not named in a charge-sheet does not constitute a final discharge. A person cannot be discharged if they were never formally an accused. The Magistrate retains the power to summon such an individual later in the same proceeding if evidence emerges against them, as this is part of the duty to identify all offenders after taking cognizance of the offence itself.

issue.issue_text: Whether proceedings against an accused, who was summoned by the Magistrate after taking cognizance of an offence based on a police report that did not name him, are considered to be instituted on a police report under Section 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The police investigated a case against the appellant and others but, accepting the appellant's alibi, filed a charge sheet (a police report) that did not name him.
Based on this police report, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate took cognizance of the offence.
The case was transferred to another Magistrate who, after examining witnesses, found evidence against the appellant and issued a warrant to summon him.
The appellant was to be tried along with the other accused under the procedure specified in Section 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The appellant argued that since he was not named in the police report, the proceeding against him was not 'instituted on a police report' and therefore Section 207A should not apply.
law: Under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence upon a police report.
Section 207A of the Code specifies the procedure for proceedings that are 'instituted on a police report'.
The crucial legal principle established by the Court is that a Magistrate takes cognizance of an 'offence', not of the 'offenders'.
Once cognizance of an offence is taken, it is the Magistrate's duty to identify all the persons who appear to be involved.
application: The Court determined that the entire proceeding was initiated or 'instituted' at the moment the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence based on the police report, as per Section 190(1)(b).

The Court rejected the appellant's argument that a separate proceeding was instituted against him when he was summoned. Instead, it held that the act of summoning an additional accused is merely a part of the original proceeding that was already instituted.

The Court reasoned that since the Magistrate takes cognizance of the offence itself, not just the individuals named by the police, his power is not limited to the accused sent up in the police report.
Once cognizance is taken, the Magistrate has a duty to proceed against any person who appears to be an offender based on the evidence, even if that person was not originally named by the police.

Therefore, because the initial cognizance was based on a police report, the entire case, including the proceedings against the subsequently summoned appellant, is considered to be 'instituted on a police report'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the proceedings against the accused were indeed instituted on a police report. The Court's reasoning was that a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence, not the specific offenders named in the report. Consequently, the summoning of an additional accused is part of the same proceeding that was initiated by the police report, and the procedure under Section 207A was correctly applied.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the initial refusal by a Magistrate to summon an individual not named in the police charge-sheet amounts to a final discharge, barring subsequent summoning in the same case.
appellant_arguments: The initial refusal by the Magistrate to summon the appellant was a judicial act that amounted to a final discharge.
respondent_arguments: There can be no question of a discharge when the appellant was not sent up for trial or named as an accused in the charge-sheet submitted by the police.

arguments.issue_text: Whether proceedings against an accused, who was summoned by the Magistrate after taking cognizance of an offence based on a police report that did not name him, are considered to be instituted on a police report under Section 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The proceeding against the appellant was not instituted on a police report under Section 207A because his name was not in the charge sheet.

The proceeding was instituted later when a warrant was issued, based on evidence taken before the Magistrate, and therefore should follow the procedure for cases instituted otherwise than on a police report (s. 207(b)).
respondent_arguments: The proceedings were correctly instituted under Section 207A because when a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence based on a police report, they take cognizance of the offence itself, not just the specific offenders named.
The summoning of an additional accused is part of the single proceeding initiated by the Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence on the police report.

cases.case_name: Pravin Chandra Mody v. State of A.P.
cases.principle: A Magistrate takes cognizance of the offence and not the individual offenders. If, after taking cognizance, the Magistrate finds that persons other than those sent up by the police are involved, it is his duty to proceed against those persons as well, and the summoning of such an additional accused is part of the same proceeding.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence under Section 190(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code based on a police report, the cognizance is of the offence itself and not limited to the offenders named in the report. The Magistrate is empowered to summon and proceed against any other person who appears to be involved in the commission of that offence, and this action is considered part of the original proceeding initiated on the police report, not the institution of a new proceeding.
obiter: The Punjab High Court in h11ta v. The State( 4) and the Allahabad High Court in Ali Ullah v. The State(5) also expressed a similar view.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Once a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence based on a police report under Section 190(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code, they take cognizance of the offence itself, not merely the specific offenders named in the report. Consequently, the summoning of an additional accused, who was not sent up by the police, is considered part of the single, original proceeding initiated by the taking of cognizance, and is therefore governed by the procedure for cases instituted on a police report.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that a Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence does so for the offence as a whole, not just for the specific offenders named by the police.

The determination of whether a criminal proceeding is instituted 'on a police report' under Section 207A or 'otherwise than on a police report' under Section 207(b) depends on the initial act of taking cognizance, not on when a particular accused is subsequently summoned.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that his initial non-summoning amounted to a discharge was rejected because a person cannot be discharged if they were never formally included as an accused in the charge-sheet submitted by the police.

The appellant's contention that the proceeding against him was not instituted on a police report was incorrect. The court held that the entire case was instituted on a police report when the Magistrate first took cognizance of the offence, and the subsequent summoning of the appellant was merely a step within that same proceeding.
The appellant's premise that cognizance was taken only with respect to the accused named in the charge-sheet was flawed; the court clarified that cognizance is taken of the offence itself.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that there can be no discharge without first being an accused in the charge-sheet was accepted by the court, which stated, 'there cannot be any question of discharge when the appellant was not sent up upon the charge-sheet submitted by the police.'

The court fully endorsed the respondent's position that when a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence, they are empowered to identify and proceed against all individuals who appear to be involved, not just those sent up by the police.

The respondent's view that summoning an additional accused is part of the single proceeding initiated by taking cognizance of the offence on the police report was adopted as the central reasoning of the court.
policy_considerations: Once a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence, it is the court's duty to identify the real offenders. If evidence suggests the involvement of persons not sent up by the police, it is the Magistrate's duty to proceed against them to ensure justice is served.
